hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Human ApoE4 reduced surface Apoer2 more than ApoE3 after Reelin treatment of primary rat cortical neurons in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: While Apoer2 quickly recycled in the presence of ApoE3, its reappearance on the cell surface was greatly delayed in the presence of ApoE4 (Figure 2B,C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower surface Apoer2; delayed receptor recycling)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14, exposed to HEK293-secreted human ApoE particles and Reelin; Results describe 1 h ApoE pretreatment, whereas Methods specify 30 min, followed by 30 min Reelin; surface biotinylation at 4°C and surface/total Apoer2 immunoblotting. No human brain cells were tested.

rows.Finding description: Surface-to-total receptor quantification showed lower Apoer2 surface expression with ApoE4 than ApoE3 in three independent neuronal experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Apoer2 surface levels show a higher reduction with ApoE4 than ApoE3.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower surface-to-total Apoer2 ratio)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; human cell-secreted ApoE particles followed by Reelin; surface biotinylation and immunoblot quantification of surface/total Apoer2. Methods specify ApoE 5 µg/ml and Reelin 2 µg/ml.

rows.Finding description: After three hours of neuronal exposure, more ApoE4 than ApoE3 remained associated with immunoprecipitated Apoer2 in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: The delayed recycling of Apoer2 was also apparent by the prolonged retention of cell-derived ApoE4 compared to cell-derived ApoE3 in Apoer2-containing intracellular compartments as shown by co-immunoprecipitation of neuronal lysates (Figure 2D,E).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater retained ApoE–Apoer2 association)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; HEK293-secreted human ApoE3 or ApoE4, 5 µg/ml for 3 h at 37°C; anti-Apoer2 co-immunoprecipitation from neuronal lysates and anti-ApoE immunoblot.

rows.Finding description: Without EMD87580, ApoE4 caused greater Apoer2 recycling impairment than the smaller impairment described for ApoE3 in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: As shown in Figure 4D and E, physiological concentrations of ApoE3 (5 µg/ml) also impaired Apoer2 recycling to a small, but significant extent. This was also prevented by EMD87580 at the same concentration (3 µM) at which the effect of ApoE4 on Apoer2 recycling was completely neutralized (Figure 4D,E), suggesting that ApoE3 also, although to a minor extent, may lose solubility upon entering the early endosome, and that this is also prevented by pH lowering.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater Apoer2 recycling impairment)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; human cell-secreted ApoE3 or ApoE4, standard 5 µg/ml, followed by Reelin; no-drug comparison; surface biotinylation and Apoer2 immunoblotting.

rows.Finding description: Cell-secreted human ApoE3 and ApoE4 particles showed similar binding to immobilized mouse Apoer2-Fc, with no significant difference reported.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 and ApoE4 bind Apoer2 with similar affinity, whereas ApoE2 binding to Apoer2 is poor.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in Apoer2 binding reported)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free pull-down assay using human ApoE isoforms naturally secreted by transfected HEK293 cells and mouse Apoer2 ectodomain-Fc immobilized on protein-G beads; ApoE 0–10 µg/ml; binding for 4 h at 4°C with 1 mM CaCl2; ApoE immunoblot. No human brain cells were tested.

rows.Finding description: Surface Lrp1 levels were comparable in rat neurons exposed to ApoE3 or ApoE4 after Reelin treatment across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: By contrast, other endocytic cell surface receptors that do not bind ApoE, such as the insulin receptor (IR) or the transferrin receptor (TfR), or that do not interact with Reelin and therefore do not undergo ligand-induced endocytosis (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (Lrp1) and low-density lipoprotein receptor (Ldlr)), were not significantly affected by the presence of ApoE (Figure 2B,C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (comparable surface Lrp1)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; HEK293-secreted human ApoE3 or ApoE4 and Reelin; surface biotinylation and surface/total Lrp1 immunoblotting. Reelin does not induce Lrp1 endocytosis in this assay.

rows.Finding description: Quantification showed comparable surface-to-total Lrp1 ratios under ApoE3 and ApoE4 across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Other ApoE receptors, such as low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (Lrp1) and low-density lipoprotein receptor (Ldlr), as well as the endocytic receptor for transferrin (TfR) and insulin receptor (IR) exhibit comparable surface levels in the presence of ApoE3 or ApoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (comparable surface-to-total Lrp1 ratios)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; human ApoE3 or ApoE4 and Reelin; quantitative surface-biotinylation immunoblot assay for Lrp1.

rows.Finding description: Increasing EMD87580 concentrations progressively restored surface Apoer2 in ApoE4-treated neurons in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Increasing concentrations progressively restored normal surface recycling of Apoer2 in the presence of ApoE4 (Figure 4B,C).
rows.Finding summary: (increased NHE inhibition with apoE4 present) -> (restored Apoer2 surface recycling)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; EMD87580 pretreatment for 1 h, followed by human cell-secreted ApoE4 and Reelin; EMD87580 dose series; surface biotinylation and surface/total Apoer2 quantification. EMD87580 is not NHE6-specific.

rows.Finding description: Increasing bafilomycin concentrations counteracted EMD87580-mediated Apoer2 recycling rescue in ApoE4-treated neurons across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Figure 4F and G show that the resulting increase of the endosomal pH reverses the correction of the ApoE4 recycling deficit by EMD87580 and results in renewed impairment of Apoer2 trafficking.
rows.Finding summary: (proton-pump inhibition with apoE4 and EMD87580 present) -> (renewed Apoer2 recycling impairment)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; human ApoE4 and Reelin, EMD87580 3 µM, and increasing bafilomycin concentrations; drugs preincubated before ApoE/Reelin; surface-biotinylation Apoer2 assay. Endosomal pH was mechanistically inferred, not directly measured in this panel.

rows.Finding description: The first NHE6-targeting shRNA restored Apoer2 surface expression in ApoE4-treated neurons in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Figure 5A–D shows that of all NHEs (1 and 5 through 9) that were targeted by shRNA inhibition, only NHE6-specific shRNAs were able to completely restore Apoer2 expression at the plasma membrane in the presence of ApoE4 (Figure 5A, lane 6, 5C, lanes 8, 10, 12, and quantified in Panels B and D).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 knockdown with apoE4 present) -> (restored surface Apoer2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons; lentiviral NHE6 shRNA construct 1, corresponding to shNHE6 a/TRCN0000068828; assay 3 days after infection; human ApoE4 plus Reelin; surface/total Apoer2 quantification.
rows.Data location: Fig 5D; supplementary file elife-40048-fig5-data1.xlsx, sheet Fig5D, E4+R versus E4+R+shNHE6(1)

rows.Finding quote: ApoE-conditioned media treatment reduces the surface expression of Apoer2 in presence of Reelin in primary neurons.
rows.Finding summary: (no added apoE4 -> added apoE4) -> (lower surface Apoer2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary E18 Sprague-Dawley rat cortical neurons, DIV9–14; comparison without EMD87580; human cell-secreted ApoE4 and Reelin; surface biotinylation followed by surface/total Apoer2 immunoblotting. Standard Methods concentrations: ApoE4 5 µg/ml and Reelin 2 µg/ml.

rows.Finding quote: (A and C) shRNA knockdown of NHE6, but not other NHEs (NHE1, 5, 7, 8, 9) restores ApoE4-impaired Apoer2 recycling.
rows.Finding summary: (no added apoE4 -> added apoE4) -> (lower surface Apoer2)

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0, three-state modeling placed the maximum intermediate population at 3.75 M urea for apoE4, approximately 90%, versus 4.75 M for apoE3, approximately 80%, indicating that apoE4 formed the intermediate under milder denaturation.
rows.Finding quote: The concentration of urea at which the folding intermediate was at maximum concentration was 3.75 M for the apoE4 22- kDa fragment (90%) and 4.75 M for the apoE3 fragment (80%).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower urea concentration for maximal intermediate formation and higher maximal intermediate fraction)
rows.Experimental system: Model-derived equilibrium populations of native, intermediate, and unfolded states for recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments at pH 4.0; derived from circular-dichroism urea-denaturation curves; maxima occur at different urea concentrations.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea, apoE4 underwent more extensive pepsin cleavage than apoE3 despite producing the same fragment bands, consistent with greater apoE4 conformational exposure.
rows.Finding quote: Digestion of the apoE3 22-kDa fragment in 3.75 M urea yielded the same bands as the apoE4 digestion but with less proteolysis of the intact apoE3 fragment (Fig. 3, middle panels).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater proteolytic susceptibility at pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 250:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing; apoE4 digestion yielded seven major bands.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0, apoE4 unfolded more readily than apoE3, while both isoforms displayed plateaus consistent with stable partially unfolded intermediates.
rows.Finding quote: At pH 7.4, apoE3 and apoE4 reflected an apparent two-state denaturation. The midpoints of denaturation were 5.2 and 4.3 M urea, respectively. At pH 4.0, a pH value known to stabilize folding intermediates, apoE4 and apoE3 dis- played the same order of denaturation but with distinct plateaus, suggesting the presence of a stable folding intermediate
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater susceptibility to acidic-pH unfolding, with stable intermediates in both)
rows.Experimental system: Bacterially expressed recombinant human apoE2, apoE3, and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments; overnight urea equilibration at 4 °C in sodium acetate buffer, pH 4.0; circular dichroism at 220 nm measured at 25 °C under reducing conditions; relevant comparison is apoE4 versus apoE3.

rows.Finding description: Without urea at pH 4.0, apoE3 and apoE4 produced the same major RQQTE-starting pepsin fragment and resisted further cleavage, with no significant difference reported and no statistical test provided.
rows.Finding quote: In 0 M urea, there was one major frag- ment, which had the amino-terminal sequence of RQQTE, which corresponds to amino acids 15–19 in apoE (Fig. 3, top panels). This sequence is at the flexible amino terminus of the 22-kDa fragment that is not resolved in the x-ray structure (34). Further addition of pepsin or longer digestion times did not produce smaller cleavage products under these conditions
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in the reported pepsin-cleavage pattern without urea at pH 4.0)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 without urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 10:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0 in 4.75 M urea, apoE3 and apoE4 showed similar cleavage bands and a smaller difference in digestion extent than at 3.75 M, indicating convergence of their conformational susceptibility.
rows.Finding quote: The bands after digestion of apoE3 and apoE4 in 4.75 M urea were similar to those obtained after digestion in 3.75 M urea, but there was less difference in the extent of digestion (Fig. 3, bottom panels).
rows.Finding summary: (3.75 M -> 4.75 M urea) -> (smaller APOE4–APOE3 difference in proteolytic susceptibility at pH 4.0)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 in 4.75 M urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 2000:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing.

rows.Finding description: Urea denaturation of recombinant human apoE amino-terminal domains at pH 7.4 showed lower unfolding resistance for apoE4 than apoE3, with respective midpoints of 4.3 and 5.2 M urea.
rows.Finding quote: The midpoints of denaturation for the 22-kDa fragments of apoE3 and apoE4 were 5.2 and 4.3 M urea, respectively, consistent with previous results (22) (Fig. 1A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower urea concentration required for unfolding at pH 7.4)
rows.Experimental system: Bacterially expressed recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments; protein incubated overnight at 4 °C across urea concentrations in sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; circular dichroism at 220 nm measured at 25 °C under reducing conditions; no cells, endosomes, or lysosomes.

rows.Finding description: Three-state fitting of acidic-pH denaturation supported stable folding intermediates for both apoE3 and apoE4, without establishing an isoform difference in fit quality.
rows.Finding quote: Therefore, the data were analyzed according to a three-state model (native/intermediate/unfolded) (28), which gave excel- lent fits for the apoE3 and apoE4 isoforms (Fig. 1C) but did not give a better fit for apoE2 than the two-state model.
rows.Finding summary: Both apoE3 and apoE4 acidic-pH unfolding curves were described as excellent fits to the three-state model.
rows.Experimental system: Three-state equilibrium-model analysis of circular-dichroism denaturation data from recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments at pH 4.0; same underlying experiment as Fig. 1B.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: After 15 minutes of human ApoE treatment, primary mouse cortical neurons had lower surface Apoer2 with ApoE4 than with ApoE3, based on four independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Whereas ApoE2 (lane 2) and ApoE3 (lane 3) did not reduce surface expression of Apoer2 compared with the control (lane 1), ApoE4 significantly decreased surface expression of this “dual function” Reelin and ApoE receptor (lane 4), suggesting that Apoer2 availability, and thus function, at the cell surface might be impaired.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (lower neuronal surface Apoer2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 18 wild-type mice at 12–13 days in vitro; treatment with 3 μg/mL HEK293-secreted human ApoE3 or ApoE4 for 15 minutes at 37 °C; membrane-impermeable surface biotinylation, NeutrAvidin precipitation, and Apoer2 immunoblotting; surface Apoer2 normalized to total cellular Apoer2. Recipient cells were mouse neurons.

rows.Finding description: During Reelin costimulation, human ApoE4 produced a greater reduction of surface Apoer2 than ApoE3 in primary mouse cortical neurons.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 was marginally, but not significantly, more effective than ApoE2, whereas ApoE4 led to a dramatic and statistically highly significant reduction of Apoer2 at the neuronal cell surface.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4, with Reelin) -> (lower neuronal surface Apoer2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 18 wild-type mice at 12–13 days in vitro; 3 μg/mL HEK293-secreted human ApoE isoforms plus 2 μg/mL Reelin for 2 hours at 37 °C according to Fig 1C legend; surface biotinylation, NeutrAvidin precipitation, and Apoer2 immunoblotting normalized to total Apoer2. The general SI biotinylation protocol instead specifies 15 minutes. Recipient cells were mouse neurons.

rows.Finding description: Adding human ApoE4 during Reelin stimulation significantly reduced surface Apoer2 compared with the Reelin-stimulated control without added ApoE in primary mouse cortical neurons.
rows.Finding quote: All ApoE isoforms ( Fig. 1 C , lanes 2–4) significantly decreased surface expression of Apoer2 upon Reelin stimulation compared with control (lane 1).
rows.Finding summary: (no added ApoE -> ApoE4, with Reelin) -> (lower neuronal surface Apoer2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 18 wild-type mice at 12–13 days in vitro; control medium or 3 μg/mL HEK293-secreted human ApoE4 together with 2 μg/mL Reelin for 2 hours at 37 °C according to Fig 1C legend; surface biotinylation and Apoer2 immunoblotting normalized to total Apoer2. The general SI biotinylation protocol instead specifies 15 minutes. Recipient cells were mouse neurons.

rows.Finding description: In primary embryonic mouse cortical neurons exposed to human ApoE, ApoE4 showed delayed release into the medium and greater intracellular retention than ApoE3 throughout the 30–120-minute chase, providing indirect evidence for impaired receptor recycling without measuring receptor-binding strength.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with the earlier reports, ApoE4 release into the culture medium (lanes 4, 8, and 12) during the chase period was markedly delayed compared with ApoE2 (lanes 2, 6, and 10) and ApoE3 (lanes 3, 7, and 11). Substantially more ApoE4 was retained in intracellular compartments at all time points, confirming that impaired recycling of ApoE4 also occurs in primary neurons.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (delayed ApoE recycling and greater intracellular ApoE retention)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 18 wild-type mice, cultured for 12–13 days; human ApoE lipoproteins naturally secreted by stably transfected HEK293 cells, 3 μg/mL at 37 °C; suramin removal of surface-bound ApoE followed by 30-minute, 1-hour, or 2-hour chase; medium and lysate ApoE immunoblotting. Results and SI specify a 15-minute loading incubation; Fig 1A legend specifies 30 minutes. Recipient cells were mouse neurons, not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: In acutely Reelin-stimulated primary mouse cortical neurons, ApoE4 treatment reduced surface GluN2B in the ApoE isoform comparison, consistent with impaired glutamate-receptor trafficking.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE4 reduces GluA1, GluA2/3, and GluN2B cell-surface levels in acutely Reelin stimulated primary neurons.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4, with Reelin) -> (lower neuronal surface GluN2B)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic wild-type mouse cortical neurons at 12–13 days in vitro, exposed to HEK293-secreted human ApoE isoforms and acute Reelin stimulation; surface biotinylation, NeutrAvidin isolation, and GluN2B immunoblotting. The SI surface-biotinylation protocol specifies 3 μg/mL ApoE and 15 minutes at 37 °C. Supplied text does not separately assign subunits to Fig 2H versus Fig 2I. Recipient cells were mouse neurons.
rows.Data location: Fig 2H and Fig 2I, jointly described in Results and legend

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: In APOE4-treated neurons, Exo-1 inhibition showed that the APOE4-dependent increase in surface LRP1 required exocytosis, testing trafficking machinery while holding APOE4 constant.
rows.Finding quote: A) Western blot analysis from neuronal culture treated with APOE 4 or with exocytosis inhibitor Exo-1 shows that exocytosis is required for APOE4 to mediate surface expression of LRP1 (B, C).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 treatment -> APOE4 with Exo-1) -> (inhibition of APOE4-mediated surface LRP1 elevation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary mouse neuronal culture; Methods describe cortical neurons isolated from P1 pups, but panel-specific genotype is unspecified. rows.Finding quote: In contrast, APOE4 enhanced the trafficking of surface LRP1 levels (Fig. 6A–C).

rows.Finding description: Adding APOE4 to astrocyte-conditioned medium increased neuronal surface LRP1 relative to conditioned medium alone, an opposite surface-availability surrogate to impeded recycling.
rows.Finding quote: (K–M) Western blot analysis from neuronal culture treated with ACM alone (control), APOE4+ACM, and with APOE4+GPC-4 shRNA treated ACM show that APOE4-induced surface expression of LRP1 is likely mediated through GPC-4.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Human isogenic APOE3 and APOE4 astrocytes were assayed for fluorescent LDL binding with an excess unlabeled-LDL competition control, revealing significantly higher surface binding in APOE4 cells, contrary to generalized loss of surface receptor availability but without directly measuring ARF6-related recycling.
rows.Finding quote: Although LDL significantly bound more cell surface receptors (e.g. LDLRs) in APOE4 astrocytes, highlighting increased cholesterol uptake potential (Figure 6E), LDL supplementation did not increase intracellular free cholesterol in APOE4 compared to APOE3 over baseline (Figures 6B and 6C), suggesting cholesterol uptake is not the mechanism for increased cholesterol.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher cell-surface LDL binding in isogenic human astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Human fibroblast-derived hiPSC astrocytes from CRISPR/Cas9-edited isogenic APOE3/APOE4 lines of Indiv1 and Indiv2, sharing APOE haplotype hap.03; forebrain NPC-derived astrocytes harvested at 30 DIV. Cells were grown in serum-free astrocyte medium on poly-D-lysine-coated coverslip-bottom dishes for 48 h, incubated with Alexa546-labeled LDL for 5 min, washed and fixed; confocal sum-projection fluorescence was quantified per cell area. Competition controls included 2.5-fold excess unlabeled LDL.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: In cultured cells expressing fluorescently tagged APOE, APOE4 accumulated in enlarged late endosomes and lysosomes relative to APOE3, providing an accumulation surrogate for aggregation.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with previous studies showing that expression of APOE4 damages lysosomal membrane integrity, dysregulates endo/lysosomal pH, and results in enlarged endosomes in various models, we found that APOE4 accumulates in enlarged lysosomes and late endosomes (Figure 1).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased APOE accumulation in enlarged late endosomes and lysosomes)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured cell lines expressing fluorescently tagged human APOE3 or APOE4; localization in late endosomes and lysosomes. Host species, cell type, source, age, treatment duration, and detailed localization assay are not specified. Human brain-cell identity and non-aged status are not established.

rows.Finding description: Among neuronal LRP1-intact APP/PS1 mice at 9 months, APOE4 mice had more GDN-HCl-extractable insoluble hippocampal apoE than APOE3 mice, with 18–23 mice per group.
rows.Finding quote: Insoluble apoE amounts in the GDN-HCl fraction were higher in APP/PS1; APOE4 control mice than in APP/PS1; APOE3 control mice, which was not affected by neuronal LRP1 deficit ( Figure 3I ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4; neuronal LRP1 intact) -> (higher insoluble hippocampal apoE)
rows.Experimental system: Male and female 9-month-old APPswe/PSEN1ΔE9 mice with homozygous human APOE3-targeted replacement or APOE4-targeted replacement, Lrp1 floxed alleles, and no αCaMKII-Cre; hippocampal detergent-insoluble pellet extracted with guanidine hydrochloride and analyzed by protein-normalized apoE ELISA. Tissue insolubility was measured without cell-type or endolysosomal localization; these are amyloid-model mice, not non-aged human cells.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: In human HepG2 cells, DMPC-complexed apoE4-(72-166) reduced LDL binding by 55%, versus 26% for DMPC-complexed apoE3-(72-166), showing greater receptor-binding competition without measuring receptor recycling.
rows.Finding quote: Among the three isoforms, apoE4-(72-166)-DMPC complex decreased the 3H-LDL binding by 55%, comparing with 19% for apoE2-(72-166)-DMPC and 26% for apoE3-(72-166)-DMPC.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(72-166)-DMPC -> apoE4-(72-166)-DMPC) -> (greater competition for LDLR binding)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells, source unspecified, incubated with 3H-LDL and competing DMPC complexes of recombinant human apoE-(72-166) fragments expressed in E. coli; receptor-binding incubation at 4°C for 2 hours. This is a liver-derived cell system using truncated proteins; receptor recycling and endosomal dissociation were not measured.
